## Neutral on Paper, Not in Fact {.center}

> "The model is fair. It doesn't even use the protected attribute."

. . .

Then an audit shows its scores still track that attribute — perfectly.

. . .

**The number said neutral. The dependence was there.**

## What Is Fairness? {.center}

A model is **unfair** when its decision would change if we flipped only a
**protected attribute** $S$ — sex, race, age — and held everything else fixed.

. . .

Credit, hiring, bail, insurance: the score should track **risk**, not **who you
are**.

. . .

The goal, stated plainly: a prediction that **does not depend on $S$**.

## The Three Layers

::: {#2950a15d .cell fig-height='3.2' fig-width='10.5' execution_count=2}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![](04-fairness_files/figure-revealjs/cell-3-output-1.png){width=1667 height=565}
:::
:::


Bias hides in the arrows: $S$ **leaks** into the features, the model passes it to
$\hat y$. We audit the dashed link — and train to cut it.

## Fairness Is a Dependence

Most fairness criteria are statements about **dependence** between those layers.
Ours — *independence* (statistical parity):

$$\hat y \perp S \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \operatorname{Dep}(\hat y, S) = 0$$

. . .

That turns a moral word into a **measurable quantity** — the very dependence
measures from Module 1, now used to *audit* and to *train*.

. . .

*(Other criteria condition on the true label — equalized odds, sufficiency — but
all are dependence statements.)*

## The Standard Check Is Blind

::: {#90cde735 .cell fig-height='3.8' fig-width='10' execution_count=3}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![](04-fairness_files/figure-revealjs/cell-4-output-1.png){width=1943 height=703}
:::
:::


Correlation sees straight lines. The bend lives where it can't look.

## Two Framings, One Operation {.center}

**Fairness** — a credit model must not depend on a protected attribute $S$.

. . .

**Factor-neutrality** — a strategy must not load on the market factor $S$.

. . .

"Don't discriminate" and "don't load on the factor I'm hedging" are the
**same maths**: drive $\operatorname{Dep}(\hat y, S) \to 0$.

## The Objective — The Whole Module in One Line

Perfect neutrality ($\operatorname{Dep}=0$) usually costs accuracy — so don't
demand it, **trade it off**:

$$\text{loss} = \underbrace{\text{fit}(\hat y, y)}_{\text{predict well}}
+ \mu \cdot \underbrace{\operatorname{Dep}(\hat y, S)}_{\text{stay blind to } S}$$

. . .

- $\mu$ dials accuracy ↔ neutrality
- every method ahead is one **choice of $\operatorname{Dep}$** (from Module 1)

---

## #1 Drop the Feature — And Watch It Fail

The naive fix: delete $S$. But other features **proxy** for it.

::: {#dad052d0 .cell fig-height='3.6' fig-width='10' execution_count=4}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![](04-fairness_files/figure-revealjs/cell-5-output-1.png){width=1943 height=662}
:::
:::


**You cannot remove a dependence you refuse to look at.**

## #2 Linear Neutrality — Leaves the Curve

Orthogonalize against $S$ (the beta-neutral classic):

$$r = \hat y - \frac{\operatorname{Cov}(\hat y, S)}{\operatorname{Var}(S)}\,S
\quad\Rightarrow\quad \operatorname{Cov}(r, S) = 0$$

. . .

But zero covariance ≠ independence. If $\hat y = S^2$, then
$\operatorname{Cov}(S^2, S) = 0$ for symmetric $S$ — **fully dependent, looks
neutral.** The Module-1 hole returns.

## #2 Linear Neutrality — In Pictures

::: {#884936d5 .cell fig-height='3.6' fig-width='10' execution_count=5}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![](04-fairness_files/figure-revealjs/cell-6-output-1.png){width=1943 height=662}
:::
:::


Pearson → 0, but the curve (and the CKA) survives.

## #2.5 The Tempting Shortcut: Gaussianize First {.center}

*Hope:* per-variable Gaussianize everything → linear methods suffice.

. . .

*Reality:* **marginal** Gaussianization leaves the nonlinear $\hat y$–$S$
relation intact.

. . .

*The real fix:* a **conditional** transform — Gaussianize $\hat y$ *given* $S$ —
actually removes it. (Joint RBIG only decorrelates the *pair*; its $\hat y$-axis
still encodes $S$, so it isn't a fair model.) Simpler still: the penalty, next.

## #2.5 Watch the Shortcut Fail

Gaussianize each axis on its own and the bend — and the CKA — barely move. Only a
**conditional** map removes it.

::: {#8918a303 .cell fig-height='3.3' fig-width='11' execution_count=6}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![](04-fairness_files/figure-revealjs/cell-7-output-1.png){width=2143 height=604}
:::
:::


Marginal Gaussianization barely bends the trend (CKA holds); only conditioning
on $S$ flattens $\mathrm{E}[\hat y \mid S]$ — genuine independence.

## #3 The CKA Penalty — A Measure That Sees Curves

The fix is the measure. **CKA** is the normalized HSIC from Module 1:

$$\operatorname{CKA}(\hat y, S) =
\frac{\operatorname{HSIC}(\hat y, S)}
     {\sqrt{\operatorname{HSIC}(\hat y,\hat y)\,\operatorname{HSIC}(S, S)}}
\in [0, 1]$$

- Sees **nonlinear** dependence — the curve that fooled Pearson
- **Bounded** in $[0,1]$ → $\mu$ is interpretable
- **Differentiable** → you can train against it

## #3 Learn the Model, Penalize the Dependence

Now the objective from the start is concrete — just set $\operatorname{Dep} =
\operatorname{CKA}$:

$$\text{loss} = \underbrace{\text{fit}(\hat y, y)}_{\text{predict well}}
+ \mu \cdot \underbrace{\operatorname{CKA}(\hat y, S)}_{\text{stay off } S}$$

. . .

Train it end to end:

- the **fit** term pulls $\hat y$ toward the target $y$
- the **CKA** term pushes $\hat y$ off $S$ — *curves included*
- $\mu$ sets who wins; sweep it to trace the trade-off

## #3 The CKA Penalty — Before & After

Fit once with $\mu=0$, once with $\mu=8$; plot $\hat y$ against $S$ each time and
watch the bend flatten:

::: {#230fa063 .cell fig-height='3.2' fig-width='10' execution_count=7}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![](04-fairness_files/figure-revealjs/cell-8-output-1.png){width=1943 height=582}
:::
:::


Left bends with $S$; right is flat — same model, one extra penalty term.

## #4 Adversarial — The Learned Dep {.center}

Don't *fix* the measure — **learn** it: a probe tries to recover $S$ from $\hat
y$; the model trains to defeat it.

. . .

When the probe fails, the predictions are independent of $S$ *by definition*.

. . .

The flexible extreme — adapts to any structure, at the cost of unstable min-max
training.

## The Scorecard — The Trade-Off Curve

::: {#0db296c2 .cell fig-height='4.2' fig-width='8' execution_count=8}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![](04-fairness_files/figure-revealjs/cell-9-output-1.png){width=1543 height=786}
:::
:::


Read it right to left: across the flat top neutrality is nearly **free**; past
the **elbow**, every further drop in CKA costs real accuracy.

## Reading the Frontier — Pick Your μ

That elbow is why the curve is a **menu, not an answer**. There is no single "fair
model" — you choose where on it to stand.

. . .

- **Before the elbow** — free lunch: take the neutrality, you barely pay accuracy.
- **After the elbow** — you are spending real accuracy for the last slivers of
  neutrality.

. . .

*Where to stand is a policy and ethics call, not a maths one — the maths only sets
the menu.*

## The Punchline → Lab {.center}

The same penalty, on **real data**:

. . .

A credit model that drops `sex` still leaks it through proxies — until the CKA
penalty closes the gap.

. . .

The *identical* code makes a strategy **market-neutral** — fairness and
factor-neutrality are one operation.

. . .

*Next: stop removing dependence — start [propagating](03-uncertainty.qmd) it.*
